1	\section{Related Work}
2	\label{sec:related_work}
3	
4	\paragraph{Training-free LLM IE.}
5	Training-free LLM IE spans instruction tuning \cite{instructuie-2023}, code-style schema encoding \cite{knowcoder-2024,codeie-2023}, annotation-guided extraction \cite{gollie-2024,adelie-2024}, schema-driven decoding \cite{slot-2025,oneke-2025}, and constrained JSON decoding \cite{json-schema-bench-2025}. For NER, methods include zero-shot decomposition \cite{xie-zeroshot-ner-2023,promptner-2023}, distillation \cite{uniner-2024}, and bidirectional encoders \cite{gliner-2024,gliner2-2025}. For RE, recent work examines zero-shot relation triplet extraction via prompting \cite{relationprompt-2022} and revisits relation extraction in the LLM era \cite{wadhwa-re-llm-2023}. Recent work also explores LLM-based data annotation for NER \cite{bogdanov2024nuner,zhang2023llmaaa} and self-improving zero-shot extraction \cite{xie2024selfimproving}. These methods perform well with moderate schemas (4--20 types) but none investigates how performance degrades as schema complexity scales, nor proposes quantitative metrics for inter-type confusability.
6	
7	\paragraph{Schema complexity in IE.}
8	The most directly related work is LLM-PEE \cite{llm-pee-2025}, which partitions large event schemas by type embedding similarity. Our work differs in three ways: (1)~we conduct controlled analysis to understand \emph{why} extraction degrades rather than developing an engineering solution; (2)~our BCS-controlled experiments isolate count from confusability, which LLM-PEE conflates; (3)~our SDGD experiments reveal that merge amplification (not partitioning quality) is the bottleneck in decompose-then-merge pipelines. Specifically, LLM-PEE employs union merge across sub-schema extractions, which our \S\ref{sec:sdgd} analysis shows causes precision to collapse from 0.56 to 0.21 in NER as false positives accumulate across passes; RE avoids this because closed-set classification does not require span reconciliation, explaining why LLM-PEE's decomposition succeeds for relation/event tasks but faces unresolved merge challenges on span-level extraction. Other approaches address schema complexity via hard negative mining \cite{iepile-2024}, schema definition optimization \cite{parse-2025}, multi-agent debate \cite{crossagentie-2025,cmas-ner-2025}, schema-aware decomposition for event extraction \cite{dee-2024}, and active prompting \cite{reflect-learn-2026}; all treat it as an engineering problem rather than isolating the underlying degradation factors. Concurrently, \citet{haystack-to-needle-2025} reduces label spaces via iterative LLM filtering, an engineering complement to our analytical approach. Our framework explains \emph{why} such reduction works: it implicitly lowers batch confusability.
9	
10	\paragraph{Schema complexity in dialogue and IE.} The Schema-Guided Dialogue dataset~\cite{rastogi2020towards} and SGD-X~\cite{lee2022sgd} document performance degradation with schema linguistic variation. \citet{li2023evaluating} observe count-dependent degradation in ChatGPT IE. \citet{volkanovska2025ner} categorize LLM NER errors including type confusion. The relationship between label similarity and classification confusion has precedent in traditional ML: hierarchical classification suffers sibling confusion proportional to inter-class proximity \citep{deng-2010-imagenet}, label confusion matrices improve text classification \citep{guo-2021-label-confusion}, and classification confusion captures semantic similarity \citep{zhou-2025-rethinking}. Hierarchical label sets reduce class confusion in zero-shot image classification \citep{novack-2023-chils}; enriched type descriptions improve zero-shot NER \citep{cocchieri-2025-zeroner}, both orthogonal to our confusability-aware batching.
11	
12	\paragraph{SCS novelty.} SCS shares its formal definition (pairwise cosine similarity of type name embeddings) with the partitioning criterion used in LLM-PEE~\cite{llm-pee-2025} for schema decomposition. Our contribution is not the metric itself but the controlled experimental framework that isolates confusability's predictive relationship with extraction degradation, distinguishing it from the engineering use in prior work. The modest pairwise effect size ($r^2 = 1.3$--$1.7\%$) is consistent with standards for individual-difference predictors in behavioral research \citep{cohen-1988-power}, where such magnitudes are considered ``small but real'' effects that compound at the aggregate level \citep{lakens-2013-effect-size}.
13	
14	\paragraph{Embedding anisotropy.}
15	Our centrality confound (\S\ref{sec:centrality_confound}) connects to representation degeneration: embeddings collapse into narrow cones \cite{gao-repr-degen-2019,ethayarajh-contextual-2019}, but local clusters can be isotropic \cite{cai-isotropy-clusters-2021}, explaining why MAVEN's single-ontology types conflate confusability with centrality.

## Paper Overview

The paper was authored by Mosh Levy, Alon Jacoby, and Yoav Goldberg and explores the impact of input length on the reasoning performance of large language models. It was published in the Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL 2024).

## Research Focus

The paper explores the impact of extending input lengths on the capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs), noting that despite LLMs' recent advancements, their performance consistency across different input lengths is not well understood.

## Methodology

The researchers investigated this aspect by introducing a novel QA reasoning framework specifically designed to assess the impact of input length, isolating the effect of input length using multiple versions of the same sample, each being extended with padding of different lengths, types and locations.

## Key Findings

The findings show a notable degradation in LLMs' reasoning performance at much shorter input lengths than their technical maximum. Specifically, the study reveals a notable degradation in LLMs' reasoning performance as input length increases, occurring at much shorter input lengths (e.g., 3000 tokens) than their technical maximum, with an average accuracy drop from 0.92 to 0.68.

The most substantial performance drop occurs when LLMs need to collect evidence from two non-adjacent locations within a long input, indicating that the task of identifying and integrating dispersed relevant information becomes significantly harder for LLMs as input length grows.

At count 8, correlations are weaker and nonsignificant across all variants, consistent with the narrower BCS range at lower schema complexity reducing the detectable effect size. These results confirm that the confusability effect arises from schema composition, not prompt-specific phrasing.

-We define Batch Confusability Score (BCS) as the \emph{mean} pairwise SCS across all type pairs in a batch (\S\ref{sec:bcs_controlled}). An alternative definition takes the \emph{maximum} pairwise SCS within each batch, capturing the single most confusable pair. Here we compare both aggregation methods to verify that core conclusions are robust to this choice.

-\caption{BCS--accuracy regression under mean vs.\ max pairwise SCS aggregation (FewRel, 16-relation batches). Permutation test for slope equivalence across pools: MEAN $p \approx 0.60$; MAX $p \approx 0.44$. The 80-pool row is identical under both definitions because these batches were collected using mean-aggregated BCS; the MAX column reflects the same data for completeness.}

-MAX aggregation yields stronger correlations ($r = -0.637$ vs.\ $-0.467$ for 16-rel), consistent with the hypothesis that the single most confusable pair in a batch predicts substitution errors. Both definitions produce significant negative slopes across all conditions, and the permutation tests confirm no significant difference between independent and sampled pools under either definition. We adopt MEAN as the primary definition because it better represents average pairwise difficulty across all schema combinations, while MAX may overweight a single outlier pair. The choice does not affect any paper conclusion.

-\caption{BCS-controlled FewRel accuracy. Low-BCS batches contain maximally dissimilar types; high-BCS batches contain maximally similar types. The 80-relation extreme-batch gap reflects the wider BCS range; regression slopes are consistent across pools ($p = 0.60$; Table~\ref{tab:within_pool}; see \S\ref{sec:practical_magnitude} for typical-batch magnitudes). The 16-relation condition used a single extreme batch per BCS level; bootstrap CIs require multiple batches.}

-A potential confound in the cross-scale comparison is that the 16-relation and 80-relation pools contain different types, so the observed gap could reflect pool composition rather than confusability. To control for this, we draw 100 random 16-relation subsets from the 80-relation pool and evaluate under the same BCS-controlled protocol.
-\multicolumn{7}{l}{\footnotesize $^\dagger$BCS range (IQR\,=\,0.033) insufficient for regression; slope not interpretable.} \\

-\caption{Three-way BCS--accuracy analysis on FewRel. Slope: OLS of batch accuracy on BCS (bootstrap CIs, $B{=}10{,}000$). $\Delta$: accuracy gap between top- and bottom-quartile BCS batches. See Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_within_pool} for CI interpretation.}

-The within-pool slope ($-$0.401, CI excludes zero) is statistically indistinguishable from the independent 16-relation pool ($-$0.509; permutation $p \approx 0.60$). The smaller quartile gap ($-$3.92\,pp vs.\ $-$5.31\,pp) reflects the narrower BCS range within the 80-relation pool (Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_within_pool}).

-In the full 80-relation condition, natural BCS variation is insufficient (IQR${}=0.033$) to yield a detectable effect ($n=25$, slope${}=+0.221$, $p \approx 0.76$). This does not invalidate the confusability effect; the within-pool slope is significant ($p=0.027$) when BCS is deliberately varied, but establishes that natural schema sampling at this scale does not produce sufficient BCS contrast for detection.
-Table~\ref{tab:scs-ablation} compares predictive accuracy of name-only SCS against name+definition SCS across three datasets.

-\caption{Pearson correlation between SCS and empirical confusion rate. ``Def'' concatenates type name with definition before embedding. All correlations significant ($p < 0.001$). The inconsistent direction of $\Delta r$ indicates no systematic benefit from including definitions.}

-Few-NERD is the only dataset whose prompts include type definitions; for MAVEN and FewRel, prompts use type names alone, making name-only SCS a direct match to model input. The high matrix correlation (0.66--0.89) confirms that type names capture the dominant semantic structure.

-The following simulation provides an illustrative explanatory model for how pair-level effects aggregate to batch-level variance. It is not the evidence base for our claims; the observed batch-level $R^2 = 0.218$ (\S\ref{sec:practical_magnitude}) is a direct empirical measurement independent of this simulation.

-\paragraph{Setup.} We examine whether the pair-level $R^2 \approx 7\%$ (computed over non-zero confusion pairs) can aggregate to the observed batch-level $R^2 \approx 22\%$ via a Monte Carlo simulation. From the FewRel 16-relation experiment, we estimate the inter-pair SCS correlation for pairs sharing a common type ($\rho_\text{SCS} = 0.35$). For batches of $k=8$ types ($\binom{8}{2}=28$ pairs), we simulate 10{,}000 iterations: (1) generate 28 correlated pair-level effects with individual $R^2 = 0.074$; (2) average to obtain batch-level signals; (3) compute batch-level $R^2$.

-\paragraph{Results.} Simulated batch $R^2 = 0.219$ [95\% CI: 0.092--0.361], matching the observed value of 0.218. The effective amplification factor is $\sim$3$\times$, explained by signal correlation within batches preserving variance while independent noise averages out (effective degrees of freedom $\approx 3.4$, not 28).

-When the simulation uses the unconditional pairwise $r^2 = 0.013$ (computed over all type pairs including zero-confusion pairs; Table~\ref{tab:pairwise}), the simulated batch-level $R^2$ drops to $0.044$ [95\% CI: 0.001--0.151], well below the observed $R^2 = 0.218$. The analytical formula confirms: $\text{SNR} \times \text{EF} / (\text{SNR} \times \text{EF} + 1) = 0.042$ with the same effective factor $\text{EF} = 3.35$. This ${\sim}5\times$ gap reflects the dilution from zero-confusion pairs: approximately 89\% of type pairs never exhibit mutual confusion, contributing only noise to the unconditional correlation. The conditional model ($R^2 = 0.074 \to 0.219$) matches the observed value because it isolates the minority of semantically proximate pairs that actually compete during type resolution; BCS predicts batch accuracy through the density of \emph{active} confusable pairs, not uniform contributions from all pairs.

-FewRel combines 64 train-split and 16 val-split relation types into a single 80-type pool.  Train-origin types show numerically lower accuracy ($-8.8$\,pp, $p = 0.06$; see Limitations), raising the question of whether differential pre-training exposure confounds the BCS--accuracy relationship.  We test this by adding a per-batch \emph{train-origin ratio} (fraction of relation types drawn from the train split) as a covariate in the BCS--accuracy regression.

-\paragraph{Method.}  Across 213 multi-type batches ($k \geq 2$) from the batch-composition experiment (\S\ref{sec:sdgd}) and the factorial design (\S\ref{sec:bcs_controlled}), we compute $\texttt{train\_origin\_ratio} = n_{\text{train}} / k$ for each batch.  The ratio ranges from 0.40 to 1.00 (mean 0.80, reflecting the 64/80 base rate).  We fit:

-\paragraph{Results.}  The BCS partial effect is unchanged after controlling for split-origin: $\beta_{\text{BCS}} = -0.416$, $p < 10^{-16}$ (vs.\ $\beta = -0.412$, $p < 10^{-16}$ without the covariate).  Train-origin ratio is not independently significant ($\beta_{\text{origin}} = -0.057$, $p = 0.245$), and $\Delta R^2 = 0.005$.  The BCS--accuracy relationship is therefore not confounded by differential pre-training exposure at the batch level.

-Pairwise SCS distributions do not differ significantly between train-origin (64 types, mean\,=\,0.880) and val-origin (16 types, mean\,=\,0.874) subsets (Mann-Whitney $p = 0.754$, Cohen's $d = 0.081$), confirming that the train/val split does not introduce systematic confusability bias.

-The schema-induced degradation documented here is not unique to information extraction. Schema-Guided Dialogue systems (SGD/SGD-X; \citealt{rastogi2020towards}) face an analogous challenge: as the number of intent and slot types grows, dialogue state tracking accuracy declines. \citet{li2023evaluating} observed count-dependent degradation in ChatGPT-based IE, attributing it to prompt overload. Our two-dimensional decomposition offers a more refined explanation: schema size per se is not the sole predictor; rather, larger schemas increase the probability of including high-SCS pairs, which contribute disproportionately to confusion. This distinction has practical implications: a schema of 80 types with low mutual confusability may outperform a 40-type schema with clustered semantics, and suggests that confusability-aware design principles may generalize to any task where an LLM must discriminate among a prompt-specified label inventory.

-To quantify whether performance variability is attributable to random batch composition or seed-dependent model inference noise, we decompose total variance into intra-seed (batch) and inter-seed components across three seeds (42, 123, 456), each evaluated on 25 random batches per count level.

-\caption{Variance decomposition across count levels on FewRel. Batch SD is the root-mean intra-seed variance across 25 random type batches (averaged over 3 seeds). Seed SD is the standard deviation of the 3 per-seed means. Ratio = mean batch variance / seed variance. At count 80, only one batch composition exists (the full schema), so batch variance vanishes by construction.}

-\caption{Variance decomposition on Few-NERD (3 seeds $\times$ 25 batches per count level). Batch SD: root-mean intra-seed standard deviation averaged over seeds. Seed SD: standard deviation of per-seed means. Ratio = batch variance / seed variance. At count 66 (full schema), only one composition exists, so both components collapse to near-zero.}

-Intra-batch variance dominates inter-seed variance by 5--474$\times$ on FewRel (mean 125$\times$, counts 4--64) and 10--99$\times$ on Few-NERD (mean 51$\times$, counts 2--44), confirming that random batch composition is the primary source of performance variability on both tasks. Under greedy decoding (temperature${}\,=\,0$), model inference is deterministic; the inter-seed variance reflects differences in which random batch compositions each seed generates, not inference stochasticity. The wide ratio range reflects variation in how tightly seed means cluster at each count level; even the minimum ratio (5.4$\times$ on FewRel at count 16, 10.2$\times$ on Few-NERD at count 2) indicates batch composition contributes the majority of observed variance. At count 80 (FewRel) and count 66 (Few-NERD), the full schema admits only one batch composition, collapsing batch variance by construction.

\paragraph{Why does embedding similarity predict LLM confusion?}

SCS captures semantic proximity in LLMs' type-resolution space. The unconditional pair-level effect is modest ($r^2 = 1.3$--$1.7\%$, as ${\sim}89\%$ of pairs never produce mutual confusion); among active-confusion pairs, $R^2 \approx 7\%$ amplifies ${\sim}3\times$ at batch level (Appendix~\ref{app:aggregation-sim}), yielding $R^2$ of 22--53\%. We hypothesize that the NER U-shape (\S\ref{sec:count_curves}) reflects a dual-task burden absent in RE: partial schemas require simultaneous span detection and type-membership filtering; at full-schema, filtering becomes vacuous and recall recovers, confirming task-specific pathways.

BCS slope consistency across independent and within-pool conditions (permutation $p = 0.60$) provides a robustness check that is difficult to reconcile with non-uniform contamination, which would differentially affect specific type subsets.
